newsitem.title: USA: New U.S. military plan will go to Congress.
newsitem.headline: New U.S. military plan will go to Congress.

text.p: The Pentagon will send Congress a new proposal for U.S. military strategy and modest force cuts on Thursday, with lawmakers and analysts already questioning the plan in an uncertain post-Cold War era.

Pentagon officials say Defense Secretary William Cohen's quadrennial defense review proposal calls for base closings and shrinking the size of jet fighter programs, but would cut only some 60,000 troops from the 1.4 million-member military.

"The QDR will maintain our flexible superpower status for a range of missions in the near term while saving money for (arms) modernization that we need for the future," one of the officials, who asked not to be identified, told Reuters.

But defense analysts say more basic changes are needed after the Cold War. Some also warn that the expectation of $250 billion defense budgets for the long term is unrealistic because of future demands from other government programs.

Former Assistant Defense Secretary Daid Chu, now a senior official with the Rand Corporation think tank, said on Wednesday that defense budgets could dip to $200 billion in three years "unless there is a significant national challenge that changes people's views."

Members of Congress, who voted to close nearly 100 major U.S. domestic military bases in four earlier rounds of closings, are already warning that new closings are a political minefield that they will not enter.

Cohen emphasized in recent weeks, however, that the death of the Soviet Union had not ended international threats to U.S. security and that more domestic military bases must be shut to save money for new weapons.

Cohen has declined to give advance details of the QDR except to stress that the military will maintain its ability to fight two major regional conflicts at once and will keep 100,000 troops in Europe and another 100,000 in the western Pacific.

He announced to reporters on Wednesday the formation of an additional "task force on defense reform" to study further money-saving changes in Pentagon business practices and major cuts in civilian defense personnel this year.

Defense officials earlier confirmed a Washington Post report that Cohen planned to seek a cut of about 60,000 active duty military personnel, 70,000 military reservists and some 80,000 civilian defense department personnel.
The Air Force, officials said, would bear the highest portion of the active duty cuts but had won a fight to retain planned high-cost tactical fighter programs.

They said Cohen had decided to reduce by more than 300 -- but not cancel -- the planned purchase of Air Force F-22 and Navy FA-18E/F fighter jets in programs under development by Lockheed Martin Corp. and McDonnell Douglas Corp..
Cohen was expected to recommend that the Air Force's previously planned purchase of 438 F-22s be reduced to 339. The cost of that program under the full buy had been estimated at about $67 billion.

He was also expected to recommend that Navy buys of the advanced FA-18E/F be cut to about 785 or perhaps fewer from 1,000. The Navy had planned to buy 1,000 of the aircraft for about $80 bilion by the year 2015.
Officials said there was also no indication that Cohen planned to seek cuts in the so-called Joint Strike Fighter program which Lockheed Martin and Boeing Co. are competing to build.

The winning firm is expected to eventually build as many as 3,000 of the joint strike fighters for more than $170 billion in the next century. Variations of the jet would go to the Air Force, Navy, Marines and British Royal Navy and could be sold to other countries.
